4 Free-choice Assignment: LabPrepMapper 4.1 Choosing a New Data Science for Biology Skill For my free-choice assignment, I want to learn Python programming and explore how AI can support laboratory preparation. I plan to use Python together with LangChain and Ollama. My goal is to develop a small prototype called LabPrepMapper. As a Life Sciences student training to become a biomedical laboratory scientist, I am interested in both molecular biology and data science. During Data Science for Biology 1 and 2, I learned to program in R and Bash. I would also like to learn Python because it is widely used in data science and has many applications in Life Sciences. In addition, I am interested in AI applications and in how they can be connected to existing programming tools to perform specific tasks. I do not aim to become a Python expert within this assignment. Instead, I want to learn the Python skills that are necessary to build and understand a small working application. I will therefore learn relevant Python concepts alongside the development of LabPrepMapper, rather than completing a large part of a Python course before starting the project. 4.2 Development of the Project Idea 4.2.1 Initial idea My initial idea was to develop a locally run AI assistant that could help students prepare laboratory protocols. The user would provide a protocol as a PDF document, for example, exported from LabArchives. Python functions would scan the document for a selection of predefined, safety-related topics. Examples include: Whether H-statements and P-statements are mentioned. Whether personal protective equipment is documented. Whether first-aid information and emergency procedures are included. Whether waste disposal is addressed. Whether relevant safety documentation, such as an SDS, is referred to. If a topic could not be detected, LabPrepMapper would flag it as something the student may want to review. A flag would not automatically mean that information is missing or that the protocol is incorrect. The intention was to support students in organising their preparation and noticing topics that deserve attention. 4.2.2 Teacher feedback and further reflection I discussed this idea with my teacher. The teacher suggested making the scope smaller by focusing on the chemicals used in a protocol and looking up their H- and P-statements and relevant safety information in a limited selection of reliable sources. This was a useful suggestion because it offered a concrete way to connect laboratory preparation with Python functions and an AI model. After considering the suggestion further, I reflected on the role I wanted LabPrepMapper to have. I do not want students to treat an AI-generated output as a replacement for their own preparation or for checking the original documentation. I also realised that automatically interpreting and combining safety information from different documents could make the prototype more complex than I can reasonably validate within the available 32 hours. Differences between documents may depend on the exact product, its composition or the document version. A simple summary could give an unjustified impression that the information has been fully checked. For this reason, I have decided to return to a refined version of my original idea. LabPrepMapper will focus on mapping and organising safety-related topics that are mentioned in a laboratory preparation document, and highlighting topics that may need the user’s attention. It will not independently determine whether a protocol is safe, complete or correct. It will also not generate chemical-specific safety instructions. This is a deliberate scope decision based on my own reflection about what would be useful, realistic and responsible to develop within the available time. The teacher’s suggestion helped me think more specifically about the safety-related purpose of the tool, even though I have chosen a different technical implementation for the first prototype. 4.3 Aim and Intended Functionality The aim of LabPrepMapper is to support students when preparing a laboratory protocol by creating a structured overview of selected topics in their document. It is intended as a preparation aid, not as an automated safety assessment or approval system. The first prototype will have the following workflow: The user provides a text-based PDF or a text file containing a laboratory preparation document. Python extracts the text and keeps track of the page on which it was found. Custom Python functions search for predefined terms and patterns related to selected document topics. The program records which topics were detected and on which pages they appeared. A locally running language model, accessed through LangChain and Ollama, can turn the checklist results into a short, readable summary. LabPrepMapper saves the results as a structured Markdown report for the user to review. The first set of topics will be limited to: References to H-statements and P-statements. Personal protective equipment. First aid and emergency procedures. Waste management. Ventilation and the work environment. References to SDS or other safety documentation. The exact search terms and patterns will be defined in Python and can be adapted during testing. The program will report where it detected a term or pattern. It will not decide whether the information is adequate. For example, detecting the word “gloves” does not establish that the correct protective equipment has been specified. Likewise, not finding a particular keyword does not prove that the topic is absent; the document may use different wording. The AI component will be used to summarise the checklist findings in clear language. In the first version, the language model will receive the structured checklist results rather than the full experimental procedure. This keeps the AI component focused on organising the findings and reduces the chance that it will interpret experimental details as safety advice. 4.4 Scope and Responsible Use To keep the project manageable and to make the output clear to users, the first prototype will have several limitations: It will search for predefined terms and patterns; it will not understand every possible way of describing a safety topic. It will not assess whether a protocol is safe, scientifically correct or complete. It will not determine which H-statements or P-statements apply to a particular chemical. It will not generate chemical-specific handling, storage, personal protective equipment, first-aid or waste-disposal instructions. It will not automatically compare or combine information from multiple SDS documents. A detected mention is not proof that the topic has been adequately addressed, and a missing match is not proof that the topic is absent. The AI-generated summary may contain mistakes and must be checked against the program’s actual findings. The user remains responsible for reviewing the original protocol, consulting the applicable institutional documentation and discussing uncertainties with a qualified supervisor. LabPrepMapper is intended to make preparation more structured and to encourage critical review, not to replace it. The prototype will initially focus on text-based PDFs. Scanned documents and optical character recognition are outside the first scope. Testing will use fictional documents or documents that are explicitly approved for this purpose. Any example shared in the public portfolio will be synthetic or anonymised and will not contain personal, confidential or restricted laboratory information. 4.5 Learning Objectives and Technical Approach I will learn and apply the following skills: Python fundamentals: variables, strings, conditions, loops, functions and working with lists and dictionaries. File handling: reading text files and extracting text from text-based PDFs. Text processing: searching for predefined terms and simple patterns. Error handling: dealing with missing, unsupported or unreadable files. Ollama: running a small language model locally. LangChain: connecting the local model to Python code and exploring how Python functions can be made available as tools. Testing and evaluation: checking whether the program detects expected topics and whether the generated summary accurately reflects the checklist output. Python will form the basis of the application. I will use the pypdf package to extract text from PDF files. I will use Ollama to run a small local language model and the langchain-ollama integration to communicate with it through LangChain. The first working version is a Python application with a local model call. It is not yet a fully autonomous agent. I will explore LangChain tool calling as part of the assignment, but I will only add it if I can implement and explain it reliably within the available time. A clear and testable application is more important than adding agentic functionality that I cannot properly validate. 4.6 Current Progress (26 November 2026) I started working on Python later than I originally intended because of the workload from other course components and the parallel Projecticum. I have decided to adapt the learning process instead of first completing a large part of the Python MOOC before beginning the application. So far, I have: Studied approximately two hours of Python, including introductory material and part of the next section of the MOOC. Installed Visual Studio Code, Python and the Python extension. Created a project folder and a virtual environment for LabPrepMapper. Installed Ollama and downloaded a small local language model (Qwen 3.5 2B). Installed the Python packages for LangChain, the Ollama integration and PDF processing. Created an initial Python script that reads a text file and extracts protocol steps. Tested a connection between Python, LangChain and the local Ollama model. The first test successfully read a fictional text protocol, extracted its steps and sent them to the local model for a basic overview. This showed that the main tools can communicate with each other. The next development step is to implement the predefined checklist and test PDF text extraction. 4.7 Planning and Approach A total of 32 hours is allocated to the free-choice assignment. Since I started later than planned and have already made progress with the setup and first prototype, I have changed my approach. I will learn Python concepts alongside development and focus on the skills that are directly relevant to the next part of the application. This is an adaptive approach: I will use the MOOC as a reference and learning resource, but I will not complete every exercise if I already understand and can apply the relevant concept. When I encounter a Python concept that I need for the application, I will study that topic and apply it directly. This should make the learning process more efficient and help me build a working product within the available time. 4.7.1 Distribution of Available Time Activity Planned time Current status Learning relevant Python fundamentals and MOOC topics 5 hours In progress; approximately 2 hours completed Setting up Python, VS Code, Ollama and the local model 2 hours Completed; actual time will be recorded in the work log Learning and applying LangChain with Ollama 3 hours Started; a basic model call has been tested Defining the checklist topics and creating test documents 2 hours Initial scope defined; test documents to be refined Developing Python functions for file reading and checklist scanning 7 hours Initial text-file reader and step extraction tested Creating the report and improving the application 4 hours Planned Testing, troubleshooting and evaluating the prototype 5 hours Planned Documenting the code, results and reflection 4 hours In progress through this portfolio description Total 32 hours The hours are estimates within the 32-hour limit. I will record the time actually spent, including time spent troubleshooting. If a task takes less time than expected, I can use the remaining time for testing or documentation rather than adding unnecessary features. 4.7.2 Updated Implementation Schedule The schedule below reflects the later start and the other course deadlines. My aim is to complete the main development and documentation by 20 December, so that I do not need to rely on the Christmas holiday for unfinished work. The exact working days remain flexible. Period Activities Estimated time 23–29 November 2026 Set up the environment, test Ollama and LangChain, create the first Python script, and study the most relevant Python basics. 4 hours 30 November–6 December 2026 Study dictionaries and file handling; develop the document-reading and checklist functions; test the functions with a fictional text document. 7 hours 7–13 December 2026 Add text-based PDF support, improve the checklist output, connect the results to the local model and create a Markdown report. 8 hours 14–20 December 2026 Test different documents, troubleshoot, evaluate limitations, refine the code and complete the portfolio documentation. 9 hours Planned total 28 hours I am keeping up to four additional hours available within the 32-hour allocation for unexpected problems or improvements. I aim not to use this buffer unless necessary. This schedule is adapted to the progress made so far and may be adjusted if other course work requires more time. 4.8 Requirements To complete the assignment, I will use: A computer capable of running Python and a small Ollama model locally. Visual Studio Code as the development environment. Python and a project-specific virtual environment. Ollama with a small local language model. The langchain and langchain-ollama Python packages. The pypdf package for extracting text from PDF documents. Fictional or explicitly approved, anonymised test documents. 4.9 Development and Final Product The final product will be a self-developed Python application called LabPrepMapper. It will read a text-based laboratory preparation document, search for selected safety-related topics, record where those topics are mentioned and generate a structured report. A local language model, accessed through LangChain and Ollama, will help summarise the checklist findings in readable language. The prototype will demonstrate my ability to use Python for file processing, text analysis, data structures and custom functions. It will also demonstrate how a locally running language model can be connected to a Python application. If time and technical feasibility allow, I will explore a limited tool-calling step through LangChain. This is an additional learning goal rather than a requirement for the first working version. I will test the program using fictional or approved documents with known examples of topics that should be detected. I will compare the output with the document manually to see whether the expected terms and pages are found. I will also test cases where a topic is not mentioned, where alternative wording is used, and where a file cannot be read. I will evaluate false matches, missed matches, PDF extraction problems and whether the AI summary accurately reflects the checklist results. The final evaluation will focus on the technical performance and limitations of the prototype. It will not attempt to validate the safety of a laboratory protocol. Possible improvements for future development may include better recognition of alternative wording, a more user-friendly interface or, after further discussion and validation, a carefully limited way of pointing users towards approved reference documentation. 4.10 Reflection on the Development Process and Use of AI During this assignment, I have adjusted the original plan based on teacher feedback, further reflection and the technical work carried out so far. Initially, I expected to spend the first part of the assignment mainly learning Python and only start developing the application later. I realised that this would not be the most efficient approach for my goal. I therefore started building a small prototype while learning the Python concepts needed for each component. I also refined the intended role of LabPrepMapper. The initial concept and the teacher’s suggestion both focused on making safety-related information easier to find. After considering the responsibility of the user and the available development time, I chose to make the first version a document preparation aid that maps and flags topics rather than an application that interprets safety information or judges whether a protocol is safe. This keeps the tool useful while making its limitations clearer. Generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, are used as learning and development support. They may help me understand Python concepts, troubleshoot errors, discuss the structure of the application and suggest code. I remain responsible for reviewing, testing and adapting the code. I will document the parts I have used, make sure I understand how they work and only include functionality that I can explain during the assessment. 4.11 References and Tools Workflows course: Portfolio assessment Python MOOC Ollama LangChain documentation LangChain Ollama integration pypdf documentation ChatGPT was used as a sparring partner to help refine the project scope, explain Python concepts and suggest parts of the code. The project idea, decisions about the intended role of LabPrepMapper, testing and final evaluation remain my responsibility. I will validate and adapt any AI-assisted code before including it in the final product.

6 Reproducible Science 6.1 C. elegans data analysis 6.2 Deep dive into an article

6 Reproducible Science In this chapter, I demonstrate how I approach different steps of the data analysis and research cycle. First, I analyse an existing dataset using R and interpret the results. After that, I will examine a scientific article, take a closer look at the R code used by the authors and evaluate how reproducible their research is. I will use these examples to practise analysing existing data, interpreting results and thinking about possible follow-up research. I will also explain my choices and findings in my own words. 6.1 C. elegans data analysis For the first part, I will analyse a dataset provided by the HU research group Innovative Testing in Life Sciences & Chemistry. The dataset contains measurements from an experiment in which C. elegans were exposed to different chemicals and concentrations. The number of offspring was measured to investigate whether the chemicals affect reproduction. The dataset was already collected and provided as an Excel file. My task is to explore the data, visualize the results and investigate what can be learned from them. 6.1.1 Data preparation First, I need to load the necessary packages and import the data into R. The readxl package provides the read_excel() function for reading Excel files. I also use tidyverse for data manipulation and visualization. Finally, patchwork allows me to display multiple plots next to each other. With the packages loaded, I can now import the dataset. # Read the data from the data folder c_elegans <- read_excel("data/CE.LIQ.FLOW.062_Tidydata.xlsx") After importing the data, I first inspect its structure. I check the number of rows and columns and select the variables that are most relevant for this analysis. dim(c_elegans) ## [1] 360 34 df <- c_elegans |> select(RawData, compName, compConcentration, expType) glimpse(df) ## Rows: 360 ## Columns: 4 ## $ RawData <dbl> 44, 37, 45, 47, 41, 35, 41, 36, 40, 38, 44, 48, 43, 50, 16, 48, 42, 41, 44, 40, 38, 41, 37, 43, 39, 34, 55, 50, 55, 42, 49, 56, 63, 60, 58, 56, 57, 57, 64, 61, 68, 60, 65, 52, 59, 67, 80, 70, 72, 85, 91, 75, 77, 65, 78, 90, 57, 70,… ## $ compName <chr> "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnapht… ## $ compConcentration <chr> "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.499", "0.… ## $ expType <chr> "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experi… # Check for missing offspring measurements sum(is.na(c_elegans$RawData)) ## [1] 5 The dataset contains 360 rows and 34 columns. The most relevant variables for this analysis are: RawData: the measured number of offspring. compName: the name of the chemical. compConcentration: the concentration used. expType: the experiment type, such as a control or chemical treatment. I also check the data types before starting the visualization. The concentration variable is stored as character data, although it should be numeric. I convert it before plotting. I also account for decimal commas in the original values. c_elegans$compConcentration <- as.numeric( str_replace(as.character(c_elegans$compConcentration), ",", ".") ) # Check whether any missing values are present after conversion sum(is.na(c_elegans$compConcentration)) ## [1] 0 6.1.2 Raw data visualization Now that the concentration variable is numeric, I can create a first scatter plot. I use the concentration on the x-axis and the number of offspring on the y-axis. Different colours represent the chemicals, while different shapes distinguish the experiment types. However, the first plot does not display all observations correctly. Something seems to be missing. This is because a logarithmic transformation cannot display a concentration of zero. To investigate this, I check how many observations have a concentration of zero or lower and which chemicals they belong to. sum(c_elegans$compConcentration <= 0, na.rm = TRUE) ## [1] 30 c_elegans %>% filter(compConcentration <= 0) %>% count(compName, expType, compConcentration) ## # A tibble: 1 × 4 ## compName expType compConcentration n ## <chr> <chr> <dbl> <int> ## 1 S-medium controlNegative 0 30 There are 30 observations with a concentration of zero. These observations belong to the negative control (S-medium). This makes sense, since the negative control does not contain a test chemical. However, I still want to include these observations in my visualization. To solve this, I determine the smallest positive concentration in the dataset and use a pseudo-logarithmic scale instead of a regular log10 scale. This allows zero concentrations to remain visible while still displaying the other concentrations on a logarithmic-like scale. # Determine the smallest positive concentration min_pos <- min( c_elegans$compConcentration[ c_elegans$compConcentration > 0 ], na.rm = TRUE ) I now recreate the plot using a pseudo-log transformation. p1 <- ggplot(data = c_elegans, aes(x = compConcentration, y = RawData, color = compName, shape = expType)) + geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.15, size = 2) + scale_x_continuous( trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans( base = 10, sigma = min_pos / 10 ) ) + labs(title = "Relation between C. elegans offspring count and chemical concentration", y = "Number of offspring", x = "Chemical concentration (pseudo-log scale)", color = "Chemical", shape = "Experiment type") + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) p1 The new plot displays the observations more clearly, including the negative control. One important detail is that the concentration units are not the same for all compounds. Most chemicals are expressed in nM, while ethanol and S-medium are expressed in percentages. Therefore, the x-axis is mainly useful for viewing the concentration range within each compound, rather than directly comparing concentrations between all compounds. Looking at the plot, some chemicals appear to show a decrease in offspring count as their concentration increases. However, the pattern is not equally clear for every chemical. At this stage, this is only an initial observation based on the visualization. 6.1.3 Normalization Next, I normalize the data using the negative control as a reference. This makes it easier to interpret the measurements relative to the same baseline. First, I calculate the mean offspring count of the negative control. I then divide all measurements by this mean to create a new variable containing the normalized values. # Calculate the mean of the negative control mean_negative <- mean( c_elegans$RawData[c_elegans$expType == "controlNegative"], na.rm = TRUE ) # Create a new column with normalized values c_elegans$RawData_norm <- c_elegans$RawData / mean_negative # Check whether the normalization worked as expected mean(c_elegans$RawData_norm[ c_elegans$expType == "controlNegative" ], na.rm = TRUE) ## [1] 1 The mean of the normalized negative control is now 1, as expected. This means that all measurements are expressed relative to the average offspring count of the negative control. I can now create a second scatter plot using the normalized values. p2 <- ggplot(data = c_elegans, aes(x = compConcentration, y = RawData_norm, color = compName, shape = expType)) + geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.02, size = 2) + scale_x_continuous( trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans( base = 10, sigma = min_pos / 10 ) ) + labs(title = "Normalized C. elegans offspring count", y = "Normalized offspring count", x = "Chemical concentration (pseudo-log scale)", color = "Chemical", shape = "Experiment type") + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) p2 6.1.4 Results and interpretation To compare the original and normalized data, I display both plots next to each other. p1 + p2 The negative control in this experiment is S-medium, while ethanol is used as the positive control. Positive, negative and vehicle controls each have a different purpose and help assess the reliability of an experiment. The negative control (S-medium) provides a baseline measurement of offspring production without exposure to a test chemical. The positive control (ethanol) is used to check whether the experiment can detect an expected biological effect. If the positive control does not produce the expected response, this could indicate a problem with the experimental setup or assay. A vehicle control is used to determine whether the solvent or medium used to deliver a chemical has an effect of its own. This is important because it helps distinguish effects caused by the test chemical from effects caused by the vehicle. By normalizing the data, all measurements are expressed relative to the average of the negative control. This sets the negative control mean to 1. A normalized value of 0.5 represents half the offspring production of the negative control mean, while a value of 1.5 represents one and a half times that amount. Normalization makes it easier to compare the responses relative to a common baseline. However, it does not remove all background variation or replace further statistical analysis. 6.1.5 Future research So, what next? A useful next step would be to investigate the dose-response relationship for each chemical. This would help determine how the response changes as the concentration increases. The R package drc can be used to fit and visualize dose-response models (Ritz et al., 2015). For each chemical, the following steps could be followed using the normalized data: Fit a dose-response model. Use the drm() function in combination with the four-parameter log-logistic model LL.4(). The concentration is used as the independent variable and the normalized response as the dependent variable. Inspect the model. Use summary() to view the estimated model parameters and plot() to display the observed data together with the fitted dose-response curve. Check whether the curve describes the general pattern in the data. Estimate the IC50. Use the ED() function to estimate the concentration associated with a 50% effect relative to the fitted response range. In the drc package, this is referred to as the ED50. The estimated value and its confidence interval should be recorded. Evaluate the results. Check how well the model fits the observed data and whether the estimate is reliable. For example, a poor model fit or a wide confidence interval would make the estimate less reliable. In short, this analysis would help describe the relationship between the concentration of a chemical and its biological effect. It would also make it possible to compare the chemicals based on their estimated effect concentrations. 6.2 Deep dive into an article For this assignment, I selected a scientific article from PLOS ONE that makes its R code and data publicly available. Since I am interested in molecular biology, I searched for an article related to gene expression. I came across a study by Word et al. (2025), which compares two different gene expression profiling techniques: TempO-seq and RNA-seq. Article reference Word, L. J., Willis, C. M., Judson, R. S., Everett, L. J., Davidson-Fritz, S. E., Haggard, D. E., et al. (2025). TempO-seq and RNA-seq gene expression levels are highly correlated for most genes: A comparison using 39 human cell lines. PLOS ONE, 20(5), e0320862. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320862 6.2.1 Research question and summary The research question is not explicitly stated as a separate question, but I would formulate it as follows: How comparable are TempO-seq and traditional RNA-seq when measuring baseline gene expression across different human cell lines? The researchers compared two gene expression profiling techniques: TempO-seq and RNA-seq. They used data from 39 different human cell lines and compared the expression levels of overlapping genes between the two techniques. Statistical methods such as Pearson correlation and principal component analysis (PCA) were used to investigate how similar the results were. They also applied relative log expression (RLE) normalization to reduce differences between the platforms. The results showed that most genes had comparable expression levels between the two methods. Of the 19,290 genes compared, 15,480 (80%) showed concordant expression levels. However, differences were found for a subset of genes, particularly those related to histone and ribosomal functions. Overall, the authors concluded that both techniques can produce comparable results for most genes, although the choice of technique can still influence the outcome (Word et al., 2025). 6.2.2 Reproducibility assessment To assess the reproducibility of the article, I used the transparency criteria described by Sumner et al. (2020). These criteria cover the availability of the study purpose, data, study location, author contact information, ethics and funding statements, and analysis code. Transparency criterion Finding Study Purpose Yes. The purpose of the study is clearly described in the introduction. Data Availability Statement Yes. A separate Data Availability section is included. Data Location The prepared data is available in the supplementary S1 file. The RNA-seq data originates from Human Protein Atlas (version 23), and the TempO-seq FASTQ files and aligned counts are available through NCBI GEO (GSE288929). Study Location Yes. The TempO-seq studies were conducted at the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in the United States. Author Review Contact information is provided for the authors, including an institutional EPA email address and a personal email address. Their institutional affiliation is also stated. Ethics Statement Yes. The article explains that the commercially available cell lines did not require ethics approval for this study. Funding Statement Yes. Funding sources are explicitly mentioned, including support from the US EPA and the NIEHS Tox21 collaboration. Code Availability Yes. The R code used for the analyses is publicly available through Figshare. 6.2.3 Reviewing the R code I downloaded the R Markdown file and the S1 dataset. Both were relatively easy to find on the article page. The R Markdown file contains over 2,500 lines of code, divided into different sections. There is not a lot of explanatory text between the code chunks. Instead, the author makes good use of comments to explain the different steps. This makes the general workflow easier to follow, although the script is quite long. The required libraries are loaded at the beginning of the document. The author first imports the TempO-seq data from Phase 1 and Phase 2 and combines these datasets. The data is then processed and normalised. Later, the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) RNA-seq data is imported as well. The author selects the 39 cell lines available in both datasets and matches the overlapping genes. This makes it possible to compare gene expression between TempO-seq and RNA-seq. After preparing the datasets, several analyses are performed, including Pearson correlations, principal component analysis (PCA), and comparisons of relative gene expression. The results are visualised using different types of plots, such as boxplots and heatmaps. Readability rating: 3/5 The code is divided into recognisable sections and contains useful comments, which makes the individual steps reasonably easy to follow. However, the script is quite long, and some parts rely on intermediate files and fixed file paths on the author’s local EPA OneDrive environment (more on this and what I decided to do in the part below). This makes it more difficult for someone else to follow and run the complete workflow. 6.2.4 Reproducing Figure 3 For reproducing one of the figures, I chose Figure 3. This figure shows boxplots of the differences in gene expression between TempO-seq and RNA-seq for 19,290 genes across 39 cell lines. The relevant part of the original code calculates the difference between the two techniques for each gene and cell line. These differences are then used to create boxplots, with the cell lines ordered according to their interquartile range (IQR). One limitation I encountered was that the original R Markdown file refers to several intermediate files stored in the author’s local EPA OneDrive environment. These files were not included alongside the downloaded code and data. Therefore, the original workflow could not be executed directly in my new R project. However, the S1 supplementary file contains prepared expression data for the 39 cell lines. I used the TR_Overlapping_data_log2EPM sheet and adapted the relevant code to use this data instead of the unavailable intermediate files. During this process, I initially encountered the error non-numeric argument to binary operator. This occurred because at least one of the selected columns contained non-numeric data. When converting the selected columns to a matrix, R treated the matrix as character data, which prevented the subtraction. I adjusted the code to select only matching column pairs containing numeric values before calculating the differences. Using the adapted script, I was able to reproduce the boxplots corresponding to Figure 3. The main analysis steps and visualisation approach were retained, while the data import and column selection were adjusted to work with the publicly available S1 dataset. The code for creating the figure is shown below. library(readxl) library(ggplot2) library(reshape2) # Import the prepared data from S1 data <- read_excel("data/journal.pone.0320862.s001.xlsx", sheet = "TR_Overlapping_data_log2EPM") # Select matching TempO-seq and RNA-seq columns tempo_candidates <- grep("\\.x$", names(data), value = TRUE) rnaseq_candidates <- sub("\\.x$", ".y", tempo_candidates) # Keep only matching pairs that contain numeric data has_pair <- rnaseq_candidates %in% names(data) tempo_candidates <- tempo_candidates[has_pair] rnaseq_candidates <- rnaseq_candidates[has_pair] numeric_pair <- vapply(seq_along(tempo_candidates), function(i) { is.numeric(data[[tempo_candidates[i]]]) && is.numeric(data[[rnaseq_candidates[i]]]) }, logical(1)) tempo_cols <- tempo_candidates[numeric_pair] rnaseq_cols <- rnaseq_candidates[numeric_pair] # Calculate TempO-seq minus RNA-seq difference <- as.data.frame( as.matrix(data[tempo_cols]) - as.matrix(data[rnaseq_cols]) ) names(difference) <- sub("\\.x$", "", tempo_cols) # Reshape the data and order cell lines by IQR melted_data <- melt(difference, variable.name = "Cell_Type", value.name = "value") iqr_order <- sort(tapply(melted_data$value, melted_data$Cell_Type, function(x) IQR(x, na.rm = TRUE))) melted_data$Cell_Type <- factor( melted_data$Cell_Type, levels = names(iqr_order) ) # Generate boxplots ggplot(melted_data, aes(x = Cell_Type, y = value)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_hline(yintercept = c(1.47, -2.09), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") + labs(x = "Cell Type", y = "TempO-seq log2(CPM+1) - RNA-seq log2(TPM+1)") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) The adapted code reproduces the boxplot distributions shown in Figure 3. The original analysis and visualisation approach were retained, while the data import and column selection were adjusted to use the prepared data from the S1 file. The original and reproduced figures are compared in one image based on the two PNG files of both plots. This was made possible again with the patchwork package. Figure 5: Comparison of the original (left) and recreated (right) boxplots. Reproducibility rating: 3/5 The authors have made both the code and relevant data publicly available, which is a strong starting point. However, the complete original script was not directly executable using only the downloaded files because it refers to intermediate files in the author’s local environment. I was able to reproduce one figure after adapting the code to use the prepared S1 data. Therefore, I consider the analysis partly reproducible, but not immediately reproducible without additional adjustments. 6.2.5 Use of AI ChatGPT was used as a supporting tool to help navigate the long R Markdown file and the S1 dataset, identify a manageable figure to reproduce, suggest code adaptations and troubleshoot an R error. I reviewed the suggestions, ran and adapted the code myself, and remain responsible for the final analysis and interpretation. 6.2.6 References Sumner, J., Haynes, L., Nathan, S., Hudson-Vitale, C., & McIntosh, L. D. (2020). Reproducibility and reporting practices in COVID-19 preprint manuscripts. medRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/2020.03.24.20042796 Word, L. J., et al. (2025). TempO-seq and RNA-seq gene expression levels are highly correlated for most genes: A comparison using 39 human cell lines. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320862 Word, L. J., et al. (2025). Supplementary S1 file: Cell line information and gene expression data used for the analysis. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320862.s001 Word, L. J., et al. R code associated with the study. Figshare. https://doi.org/10.23645/epacomptox.27341970.v1

7 TexBox: A toolbox for text utilities in R 7.1 Why TexBox? 7.2 What’s inside the toolbox? 7.3 Developing an R package 7.4 Documenting the functions with roxygen2 7.5 A vignette as a user guide 7.6 Testing and validation 7.7 Sharing TexBox through GitHub 7.8 Reflection: What I learned 7.9 Links and resources

7 TexBox: A toolbox for text utilities in R 7.1 Why TexBox? I decided to create an R package called TexBox: a small toolbox with functions for working with text. While writing reports in R Markdown, I sometimes wanted a quick way to check how much I had written. For example, I wanted to know the number of words or sentences in a text. I also wanted an easy way to remove unnecessary spaces. TexBox brings these small tasks together in one package. I mainly had students in mind when I came up with the idea. Some assignments have a maximum word, sentence or character count, and it can be useful to check these before handing in a report. I hope TexBox can make those final checks a little easier, without having to use separate tools for every task. 7.2 What’s inside the toolbox? TexBox currently contains four functions for working with text: Function What it does word_count() Counts the number of words in text sentence_count() Counts the number of sentences in text clean_text() Removes unnecessary whitespace text_summary() Combines several text statistics in one overview The functions can be used separately, depending on what the user needs. For a quick word count, one function is enough. When someone wants a more complete overview, text_summary() combines several statistics in one table. 7.2.1 1. word_count() The word_count() function counts the number of words in a character vector. It treats whitespace as the separator between words, so it can also process multiple text elements at once. word_count("Hello world!") This returns a count of 2 words. The function first checks whether the input is a character vector. It then processes each text element separately, removes unnecessary whitespace at the beginning and end, and splits the text at whitespace. Finally, length() is used to count the resulting words. An empty string returns zero, and missing values (NA) remain missing. 7.2.2 2. sentence_count() The sentence_count() function counts the number of sentences in a text. It uses periods, exclamation marks and question marks (., ! and ?) as sentence separators. sentence_count("Hello! How are you? I am fine.") This returns a count of 3 sentences. The function splits the text at these punctuation marks and counts the non-empty text parts. It can also process multiple text elements. One limitation is that this is a relatively simple way of detecting sentence boundaries. An abbreviation such as Dr. can also be interpreted as the end of a sentence. This is something I would like to improve in the future. 7.2.3 3. clean_text() The clean_text() function removes unnecessary whitespace. It replaces multiple spaces, tabs and line breaks with a single space, and removes whitespace at the beginning and end of the text. clean_text(" Hello world! ") The result is: [1] "Hello world!" This function uses gsub() to find and replace repeated whitespace. After that, trimws() removes whitespace from the start and end. This can be useful when text has been copied from different sources or contains inconsistent spacing. It is worth keeping in mind that line breaks are also replaced by spaces, so the function is intended for cleaning text rather than preserving paragraph layout. 7.2.4 4. text_summary() The text_summary() function combines several text statistics in one data frame. It reports the original text, the number of characters, the number of words and the number of sentences. text_summary("Hello world!") The result looks like this: text characters words sentences Hello world! 12 2 1 The character count includes spaces and punctuation. This function brings the other functions together: it uses word_count() and sentence_count() and adds the character count with nchar(). This means users can get a quick overview of their text without having to run each function separately. 7.3 Developing an R package I followed the package development steps from the HU Workflows Reader and the related example in R Packages: The Whole Game. The book uses a different example package, but I followed the same general workflow and applied it to my own idea, TexBox. I started by creating the package structure with usethis::create_package(). This created the basic files and folders that R expects in a package. I then used usethis::use_r() to create a separate R script for each function. For example, usethis::use_r("word_count") created R/word_count.R. Keeping every function in its own file makes the package easier to navigate and maintain. 7.3.1 Package structure The main files and folders in TexBox each have their own purpose: File or directory Purpose R/ Contains the R scripts with the four functions man/ Contains the help files generated from the function documentation vignettes/ Contains the longer user guide for the package DESCRIPTION Contains package metadata, such as its name, title, version, author, description and license NAMESPACE Defines which functions are exported for users and manages the package namespace LICENSE and LICENSE.md Contain the information for the MIT License .Rbuildignore Lists files that should be left out of the built package The repository layout below shows how these files and folders are organised in the GitHub project. Figure 5: TexBox repository layout I also chose the MIT License. This is a permissive open-source license that allows others to use, copy, modify and distribute the code, as long as the required copyright and license notices are kept. The DESCRIPTION file is important because it tells R and other users what the package is, who created it and what it is for. It also records package details such as the version and license, and can list other packages that are needed. The four TexBox functions use functions from base R, so they do not need an additional package to perform the text operations. The NAMESPACE file has a different role: it controls which functions are available to package users. For TexBox, I marked all four functions with @export, so users can call them after loading the package. 7.4 Documenting the functions with roxygen2 I used roxygen2 to document the four functions. Roxygen2 allows documentation to be written directly above a function as special comments that start with #'. This keeps the explanation close to the code it describes. For example, the documentation for word_count() includes a short description, an explanation of its input and output, an example and an export tag. A simplified part of the comments looks like this: #' Count the number of words in text #' #' @param text A character vector containing text. #' @return The number of words in each text element. #' @examples #' word_count("Hello world!") #' @export word_count <- function(text) { # function code goes here } The main tags I used were: Tag Purpose @param Describes the function’s input arguments @return Describes what the function returns @examples Provides an example of how to use the function @seealso Links to related functions @export Marks the function as available to package users The comments start with #', which makes them different from regular R comments that start with #. After writing or updating these comments, I ran: devtools::document() This processes the roxygen2 comments and automatically generates the .Rd help files in the man/ folder. It also updates NAMESPACE, including the export information for the functions marked with @export. Users can then open the help page for a function in R, for example with ?word_count. 7.5 A vignette as a user guide Besides the help page for each individual function, I wanted TexBox to have one guide that explains the package as a whole. For this, I created a vignette with: usethis::use_vignette("texbox") This created the file vignettes/texbox.Rmd. I titled the guide A Quickstart with TexBox. It introduces the package, explains what each function does and includes examples of how to use them. The code examples in the vignette can be run by users, which makes it a practical starting point for someone who has just installed the package. After installing TexBox, the vignette can be opened from R with: vignette("texbox", package = "TexBox") The vignette is different from the individual help pages: the help pages explain one function at a time, while the vignette gives users an introduction to the complete package. 7.6 Testing and validation While developing TexBox, I tested the functions individually with different types of input. For example, I checked how they handled multiple text elements, empty strings, extra whitespace and invalid input. I also checked whether the punctuation used by sentence_count() was recognised as expected. After making changes to a function, I used devtools::load_all() to load the current development version of the package into R. This meant I could test my changes without installing the package again after every adjustment. I used devtools::document() to update the generated documentation and devtools::check() to check the package as a whole. The first package checks did not go smoothly. I initially had a problem with Rtools: the version installed did not match the version required by my R installation, so R could not find the make tool needed to build packages. After installing the matching Rtools version and restarting RStudio, this problem was solved. I also received a note because the RStudio project file was included among the top-level package files. I added it to .Rbuildignore, so it would not be included in the package build. The final devtools::check() completed with: Check Result Errors 0 Warnings 0 Notes 0 This was an important final check, because it showed that the package could be built and passed the package checks without errors, warnings or notes. 7.7 Sharing TexBox through GitHub Once the package was ready, I made it available through a public GitHub repository. This allows other people, including the course lecturers, to view the source code and install the package. I used Git to track the changes, commit the package files and push them to GitHub. There was a small extra step in this process. I had initially created the package in a separate folder from the Git repository I had already connected. As a result, the new package files were not being tracked by that repository. I moved the package files into the existing Git repository and then committed and pushed them. This taught me to pay attention to the project folder and the folder that Git is actually tracking. The package can be installed directly from GitHub with: devtools::install_github( "lucasvanderheide/TexBox", build_vignettes = TRUE ) After installation, users can load TexBox and use its functions: library(TexBox) word_count("Hello from TexBox!") sentence_count("This is TexBox. It works!") clean_text(" Welcome to TexBox! ") text_summary("Hello world! Welcome to TexBox.") I tested the installation from GitHub successfully. I also checked that the installed vignette could be found using vignette("texbox", package = "TexBox"). This was important because it confirmed that TexBox was not only working in my own development project, but could also be installed and used as a package from GitHub. View the TexBox GitHub repository 7.8 Reflection: What I learned At the beginning, creating a complete R package felt like a big mountain to me. I found it difficult to know which tools and functions I needed for the final checks. Getting everything into GitHub was also more complicated than I expected, because I first had to leave the original project and later move the package files into the Git repository. The Rtools issue was another challenge, but solving it helped me understand that the tools used to build a package need to match the R version I am working with. The sentence counter also has a limitation that I have not solved yet: abbreviations with a period, such as Dr., can be counted as sentence boundaries. This is something I would like to improve in a future version. The biggest thing I learned is that an R package is not as intimidating as it first seemed. At its core, it is a set of R functions organised in a clear structure, with documentation and checks that make it easier for other people to use. I also learned that writing the function is only one part of the process. I need to check whether it works, whether it does what I intended, and whether someone else can understand and use it. Documentation and a vignette help make that possible. I noticed that I can easily feel overwhelmed when I think about building a whole package at once. Breaking the work into smaller steps made it much more manageable. Next time, I would like to sketch out the structure and the steps before I start coding. Now that I have completed a package once, I have a better idea of what the process looks like and can work from that experience. I also enjoyed the process more than I expected, and I would like to keep developing TexBox. Possible additions could include changing the capitalization of text, counting selected special characters, or adding helpers that apply Markdown formatting such as headings, bold or italic text. I would also like to improve the sentence counter so that it can recognise abbreviations more accurately. For now, TexBox is a small package, but it gives me a good starting point for building and sharing more of my own R tools in the future. 7.9 Links and resources TexBox GitHub repository HU Workflows Reader – R packages R Packages – The Whole Game
